title: Oracle Split String by Delimiter Into Rows (With Examples)
description: Oracle split string by delimiter into rows with REGEXP_SUBSTR and CONNECT BY: get the nth value, keep empty values, and split every row of a table.

sources.title: Oracle 19c SQL Language Reference: SELECT (LATERAL, CROSS APPLY, OUTER APPLY)
Oracle 19c SQL Language Reference: Hierarchical Queries

reviewNotes: Examples written from the 19c SQL Language Reference and the APEX 24.2 API reference; nothing was run, so every query and every output block (marked expected output) needs a test run, ideally on 19c and 23ai. Please check in particular: (1) the ([^,]*)(,|$) pattern with subexpr 1 returns Oracle / NULL / AWS for 'Oracle,,AWS'; (2) that a NULL skills value in the CROSS APPLY query gives exactly one row with NULL (relies on CONNECT BY always returning the root row when LEVEL <= NULL); (3) the claim that REGEXP_COUNT(NULL, ',') returns NULL; (4) the 'Works from' column in the comparison table (REGEXP_SUBSTR 10g, REGEXP_COUNT and subexpr 11g, CROSS APPLY/LATERAL 12c); (5) that Oracle 23ai/26ai still has no built-in SQL SPLIT function, since the FAQ says so; (6) the errors when APEX is not installed (article says ORA-00904 in SQL, PLS-00201 in PL/SQL); (6b) the ORA-01722 IN-list example assumes NLS_NUMERIC_CHARACTERS with '.' as decimal; with ',' as decimal '1,3' might convert to 1.3 instead, consider a footnote; (7) whether the CONNECT BY duplicate explanation matches what the editor sees on the 4-row table. Topic chosen because autocomplete shows many variants (split string by delimiter, into rows, get first/second element, by comma, by space, into columns), the site has no article on it, and ranking pages mostly show only [^,]+ on DUAL without the empty-value bug, the multi-row duplicate problem or the IN-list case. The Oracle SQL blog post on this topic returned 403 to the fetch tool, so it was not used as a source.

data.text: To split a string by a delimiter in Oracle, use REGEXP_SUBSTR to pick out each piece and CONNECT BY LEVEL to generate one row per piece. Use REGEXP_COUNT to work out how many pieces there are. This works in every supported Oracle release and needs no extra packages.

Oracle SQL has no SPLIT function, so this question comes up all the time: a comma-separated list in a column, a CSV value passed from an application, or a list of IDs for an IN clause. In this tutorial you will split a single string, get the first or second element, keep empty values in the right position, split every row of a table without duplicate rows, and use APEX_STRING.SPLIT when APEX is installed.
How splitting a string works in Oracle
The idea has two parts. First you need a way to make N rows, where N is the number of pieces in the string. Then on row number 1 you take piece 1, on row 2 you take piece 2, and so on.

SELECT ... FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= n is the usual Oracle way to generate n rows. LEVEL is a pseudocolumn that is 1 for the first row, 2 for the second, and so on. You then pass LEVEL as the occurrence argument of REGEXP_SUBSTR, which tells Oracle which match to return.
The syntax of the two regular expression functions, from the Oracle SQL Language Reference:

data.code:
REGEXP_SUBSTR(source_char, pattern [, position [, occurrence [, match_param [, subexpr ]]]])

REGEXP_COUNT(source_char, pattern [, position [, match_param ]])
data.caption: Function syntax

items.content: position: where the search starts. Default 1.
occurrence: which match to return. Default 1. The search for the next match starts at the first character after the previous match.
subexpr: which group in parentheses to return (0 to 9). You will use this to keep empty values.
REGEXP_COUNT returns the number of matches, or 0 if there is none. Number of commas plus one gives the number of pieces.

data.text: Sample table
Create this small table of job applicants and their skills. It has the four cases you meet in real data: a clean list, a list with spaces after commas, a list with an empty value, and a NULL.

data.caption: Create and load the applicants table

data.text: Split a single string into rows
Start with one literal string. This is the pattern you will reuse in every other example.

data.code:
SELECT LEVEL AS pos,
       REGEXP_SUBSTR('SQL,PL/SQL,Unix', '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL) AS skill
  FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT('SQL,PL/SQL,Unix', ',') + 1;
data.caption: Split a comma-separated string

data.text: Output (expected output). The pattern [^,]+ means "one or more characters that are not a comma", so each match is one value. REGEXP_COUNT finds 2 commas, so CONNECT BY makes 3 rows, and row n returns match n.
Use a bind variable instead of a literal
In real code the string comes from the application. Use a bind variable so you do not repeat the string and do not build SQL by concatenation.

data.code:
SELECT LEVEL AS pos,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(:csv, '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL)) AS item
  FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(:csv, ',') + 1;
data.caption: Same query with a bind variable :csv

data.text: The TRIM removes spaces, so 'Java, Python' gives Python instead of ' Python'. Leading spaces are easy to miss on screen and they break joins and comparisons later.
Other delimiters

Change the character inside the brackets. For a space use '[^ ]+', for a semicolon '[^;]+', and for a pipe '[^|]+'. Inside square brackets the pipe is a normal character, but in the REGEXP_COUNT pattern it is not, so write REGEXP_COUNT(:csv, '\|'). The common mistakes section explains why.
Get the first, second or nth element
Often you do not want rows at all. You want one value, such as the first skill, or the values in separate columns. Pass a fixed number as the occurrence instead of LEVEL.

data.code:
SELECT applicant_id,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(skills, '[^,]+', 1, 1)) AS skill_1,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(skills, '[^,]+', 1, 2)) AS skill_2,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(skills, '[^,]+', 1, 3)) AS skill_3
  FROM applicants
 ORDER BY applicant_id;
data.caption: Split a string into columns

data.text: Output (expected output; SQL Developer shows NULL as (null), SQL*Plus shows a blank). When you ask for an occurrence that does not exist, such as the third skill for Ravi, you get NULL, not an error.

Now look at Meena, applicant 3. Her string is 'Oracle,,AWS': the second value is empty and AWS is the third value. But the query reports AWS as skill 2. The next section explains why and how to fix it.

data.title: First element without regular expressions
data.text: For only the first value, SUBSTR(skills, 1, INSTR(skills || ',', ',') - 1) does the same job with plain string functions. Appending the comma handles strings that have no delimiter at all.
Keep empty values in the right position

The pattern [^,]+ needs at least one character, so it cannot match the empty value between two commas. It skips it, and every value after it moves up one place. For a list of tags that may not matter. For positional data, such as a CSV line where column 2 is the phone number, it gives wrong results without any error.
The fix is to match "zero or more non-comma characters, followed by a comma or the end of the string", and return only the first group:

data.code:
SELECT LEVEL AS pos,
       REGEXP_SUBSTR('Oracle,,AWS', '([^,]*)(,|$)', 1, LEVEL, NULL, 1) AS skill
  FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT('Oracle,,AWS', ',') + 1;
data.caption: Keep empty values

data.text: Output (expected output). How it works:

items.content: ([^,]*) is group 1: any number of non-comma characters, including none.
(,|$) is group 2: the delimiter or the end of the string. It is part of the match, so the next search starts after the comma.
The last argument, 1, returns only group 1, so you never see the comma.
match_param is NULL, which means default matching.

data.text: The empty value comes back as NULL because Oracle treats a zero-length string as NULL. The documentation notes that this may change in a future release, so do not write code that depends on the difference.

data.title: Which pattern should you use?
data.text: Use ([^,]*)(,|$) with subexpr 1 by default. It is correct for empty values and gives the same result as [^,]+ when there are none. Use the shorter [^,]+ only when you are sure no value can be empty.
Split every row of a table
This is where most people get stuck. Splitting a string from DUAL works, but the same query on a table returns far too many rows.
Why CONNECT BY on a table returns duplicates

data.code:
-- Do not use: returns repeated rows
SELECT applicant_id,
       REGEXP_SUBSTR(skills, '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL) AS skill
  FROM applicants
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(skills, ',') + 1;
data.caption: The common broken query

data.text: CONNECT BY builds a hierarchy. With no PRIOR condition linking a child row to its parent, every row on one level is treated as a child of every row on the level above. So Asha's level 2 row is joined under Ravi and Meena as well, and the result multiplies with each level. With four rows the output is already confusing; with thousands of rows the query can run for a very long time.
Fix for Oracle 12c and later: CROSS APPLY

Oracle 12c added CROSS APPLY, OUTER APPLY and LATERAL inline views. They let a subquery on the right refer to columns of the table on its left. Now the row generator runs separately for each applicant, so the rows cannot mix.

data.code:
SELECT a.applicant_id,
       a.name,
       s.pos,
       TRIM(s.skill) AS skill
  FROM applicants a
 CROSS APPLY (
        SELECT LEVEL AS pos,
               REGEXP_SUBSTR(a.skills, '([^,]*)(,|$)', 1, LEVEL, NULL, 1) AS skill
          FROM dual
        CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(a.skills, ',') + 1
       ) s
 ORDER BY a.applicant_id, s.pos;
data.caption: Split every row with CROSS APPLY

data.text: Output (expected output). Each applicant gets exactly one row per value. Kiran's NULL skills still produce one row: REGEXP_COUNT of NULL is NULL, so no child rows are generated, but CONNECT BY always returns the starting row. Add WHERE s.skill IS NOT NULL to drop empty values and NULL lists if you do not want them.
You can write the same thing with the standard syntax: FROM applicants a CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ...) s. Both forms behave the same here.
Fix for Oracle 11g: PRIOR SYS_GUID()
On older databases without CROSS APPLY you will often see this version. It is worth recognising in legacy code.

data.code:
SELECT applicant_id,
       LEVEL AS pos,
       TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(skills, '([^,]*)(,|$)', 1, LEVEL, NULL, 1)) AS skill
  FROM applicants
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(skills, ',') + 1
       AND PRIOR applicant_id = applicant_id
       AND PRIOR SYS_GUID() IS NOT NULL
 ORDER BY applicant_id, pos;
data.caption: Legacy method for 11g

data.text: PRIOR applicant_id = applicant_id keeps each child under its own row. But that alone makes a row its own parent, and Oracle raises ORA-01436: CONNECT BY loop in user data. PRIOR SYS_GUID() IS NOT NULL is always true, yet SYS_GUID returns a new value for each row, so Oracle does not see a loop. It works, but it is a trick. On 12c and later prefer CROSS APPLY, which says what it means.
Use a comma-separated list in an IN clause

A screen sends '1,3' and you want those applicants. Writing WHERE applicant_id IN (:id_list) does not work: the bind variable is one string value, not a list. Oracle compares the number applicant_id with the string '1,3', tries to convert it to a number and fails with ORA-01722: invalid number.
Split the string inside a subquery instead:

data.code:
SELECT applicant_id, name
  FROM applicants
 WHERE applicant_id IN (
         SELECT TO_NUMBER(TRIM(REGEXP_SUBSTR(:id_list, '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL)))
           FROM dual
         CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(:id_list, ',') + 1
       )
 ORDER BY applicant_id;
data.caption: Filter by a CSV list of IDs (:id_list = '1,3')

data.text: Output (expected output). Here [^,]+ is the right pattern, because an empty ID is meaningless. The query text stays the same whatever list is passed, so Oracle can reuse the parsed statement.
APEX_STRING.SPLIT: the shortest option
If Oracle APEX is installed in your database (it is available on Autonomous Database, for example), the APEX_STRING package has a SPLIT function that returns a collection of type apex_t_varchar2:

data.code:
APEX_STRING.SPLIT (
    p_str   IN VARCHAR2,
    p_sep   IN VARCHAR2    DEFAULT apex_application.LF,
    p_limit IN PLS_INTEGER DEFAULT NULL )
    RETURN apex_t_varchar2;
data.caption: Signature from the APEX API reference

data.text: Note the default separator is a line feed, not a comma, so always pass p_sep. A separator longer than one character is treated as a regular expression. You can query the result like a table:
Output (expected output). In PL/SQL you can loop over the collection directly:

data.caption: Loop over split values in PL/SQL

data.text: If APEX is not installed, the package does not exist: SQL reports an invalid identifier (ORA-00904) and PL/SQL reports that the identifier must be declared (PLS-00201). Use the REGEXP_SUBSTR method instead.
Which method should you use?

content: Split one string or bind value
Split every row of a table

data.text: Common mistakes

items.content: Using [^,]+ on data with empty values. Values shift position silently. Use ([^,]*)(,|$) with subexpr 1.
Running CONNECT BY LEVEL directly on a multi-row table. You get repeated rows or a very slow query. Use CROSS APPLY, or the PRIOR SYS_GUID() trick on 11g.
Forgetting TRIM. 'Java, Python' gives ' Python', which will not match 'Python' in a join.
Counting a special character with REGEXP_COUNT. In a pattern, | means OR, and . means any character. REGEXP_COUNT(str, '.') counts every character, not dots. Escape them: '\|', '\.'.

Treating a character class as a multi-character delimiter. '[^; ]+' splits on a semicolon or a space, not on the two-character string '; '. For a real multi-character delimiter, split on the first character and TRIM, or use APEX_STRING.SPLIT with a regular expression.
Passing a CSV string to IN (:list). It is one value, not a list. Split it in a subquery.

data.title: Do not store lists in one column if you can avoid it
data.text: A column like skills breaks first normal form. You cannot index the individual values, and every query has to split the string again. If you control the design, use a child table such as applicant_skills(applicant_id, skill) and build the comma-separated text with LISTAGG only for display.
Performance tips

items.content: Regular expression functions use more CPU than SUBSTR and INSTR. For a few thousand rows it does not matter. For a large batch job, test both and measure.
Filter rows before splitting. Put the WHERE conditions on the main table so the row generator runs for fewer rows.
A predicate on a split value cannot use an index on the original column. If you search by one value often, that is a strong sign the data should be in a child table.
If you split the same string many times inside PL/SQL, split it once into a collection and reuse it.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
Is there a SPLIT function in Oracle?
Not in Oracle Database SQL. The standard way is REGEXP_SUBSTR with CONNECT BY LEVEL. If APEX is installed, APEX_STRING.SPLIT gives you a ready-made function.
How do I split a string by delimiter and get the second element in Oracle?
Use occurrence 2: REGEXP_SUBSTR(str, '([^,]*)(,|$)', 1, 2, NULL, 1). This returns the real second value even when the first one is empty.
How do I split a string by space in Oracle?
Use '[^ ]+' as the pattern and count spaces with REGEXP_COUNT(str, ' '). If words can be separated by more than one space, use '[^ ]+' and count words with REGEXP_COUNT(str, '[^ ]+') instead.
Can I split a CLOB?
Yes. REGEXP_SUBSTR and REGEXP_COUNT accept CLOB values, and REGEXP_SUBSTR returns a CLOB when the source is a CLOB. Note that APEX_STRING.SPLIT shown above takes a VARCHAR2.
How do I join the rows back into one string?
Use LISTAGG, for example LISTAGG(skill, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY pos). It is the reverse of splitting.
Summary

items.content: Generate one row per value with CONNECT BY LEVEL <= REGEXP_COUNT(str, delimiter) + 1.
Pick each value with REGEXP_SUBSTR(..., LEVEL), and TRIM the result.
Use ([^,]*)(,|$) with subexpr 1 when values can be empty.
On a table, wrap the row generator in CROSS APPLY (12c and later), never plain CONNECT BY.
Split CSV bind variables inside an IN subquery to avoid ORA-01722.
Use APEX_STRING.SPLIT when APEX is installed, and always pass the separator.
If you split the same column often, move the values into a child table.

linkedin.post:
Your query works on DUAL, then returns hundreds of repeated rows when you run it on the real table. Classic Oracle string split bug.

Oracle SQL has no SPLIT function. The standard method is REGEXP_SUBSTR plus CONNECT BY LEVEL. Five things that save hours:

→ Count the pieces with REGEXP_COUNT(str, ',') + 1 and pass LEVEL as the occurrence
→ The pattern [^,]+ skips empty values, so 'Oracle,,AWS' returns AWS as item 2. Use ([^,]*)(,|$) with subexpr 1 to keep positions right
→ Never run CONNECT BY LEVEL directly on a multi-row table. Wrap it in CROSS APPLY (12c and later) so each row is split on its own
→ WHERE id IN (:list) with '1,3' fails with ORA-01722. Split the bind variable in a subquery
→ TRIM every value. ' Python' will not match 'Python'

If APEX is installed, APEX_STRING.SPLIT(str, ',') does it in one call. Pass the separator: the default is a line feed.

Do you still see the PRIOR SYS_GUID() trick in your legacy code, or have you moved to CROSS APPLY?

points: LEVEL makes one row per value
Commas plus one is the number of values
slides.code:
SELECT LEVEL AS pos,

slides.title: Empty values shift position
slides.body: [^,]+ needs at least one character, so it skips the empty value in 'Oracle,,AWS' and reports AWS as item 2. Match zero or more characters and return group 1 instead.

slides.title: Split every row: CROSS APPLY
slides.body: Plain CONNECT BY on a table mixes rows and repeats them. CROSS APPLY (12c and later) runs the split once per row.
slides.code:
SELECT a.applicant_id, s.skill
FROM applicants a
CROSS APPLY (
  SELECT REGEXP_SUBSTR(a.skills,
    '[^,]+', 1, LEVEL) AS skill
  FROM dual
  CONNECT BY LEVEL <=
    REGEXP_COUNT(a.skills, ',') + 1
) s;

slides.title: CSV list in an IN clause
points: IN (:list) with '1,3' is one string, not a list
Comparing it to a number raises ORA-01722
